summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland rests on self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality may change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar. No surgical requirement, no medical diagnosis and no court proceeding applies to the route. In the first months after introduction about 350 people had used it, according to SWI swissinfo reporting of 7 August 2022.

The treatment of minors is contested between the chambers of the Federal Assembly. The National Council suppressed the requirement for guardian consent for 12 to 18-year-olds, while the Council of States set 16 as the age below which guardian consent is needed. The wording finally in force is not resolved by the available sources.

Same-sex marriage has been in force since 1 July 2022 under the Marriage for All reform, which also opened adoption and assisted reproduction to same-sex couples; 64.1% of voters approved the reform in referendum.

On hate speech, since 1 July 2020 public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is punishable under Art. 261bis of the Swiss Criminal Code. Switzerland has no general hate-crime provision: bias-motivated offences are addressed through anti-discrimination provisions. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report records that Swiss police do not record bias motivation and that national recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other offences.

Reported anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crime is at a sustained level and rising. Monitoring by the LGBTIQ Helpline indicates roughly six anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crimes reported per week, 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030, built on three pillars: support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence. Implementation is coordinated by the Federal Office for Gender Equality.

Placement of transgender detainees is governed cantonally. There is no federal provision on trans placement in detention, no Federal Supreme Court case law on the subject, and no trans-specific units or federal solitary-confinement practice for trans prisoners. The canton of Basel-Stadt added gender identity to its detention law (JVG), adopted by the Grand Council on 13 November 2019: §2 separates female and male detainees while stating that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, and allows the prison directorate to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority.

Employment is governed by Art. 328ff. of the Code of Obligations, which requires employers to protect employees' personal dignity, concretised for trans people by the Equality Act (GLG). Trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any change to official documents.

Conversion therapy remains unregulated at federal level. The National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 by 143 votes to 37 with 11 abstentions, but the bill is still pending in the Council of States. Cantonal bans exist in Neuchâtel (2023), Valais and Vaud (2024). The Federal Council states such therapies are ineffective and cause significant suffering to young people subjected to them, and would breach professional duties.

In June 2023 the Federal Supreme Court upheld a cantonal school's dismissal of a teacher who refused to call a transgender student by his chosen male first name, ruling that the school's duty to protect the student's privacy and self-determination outweighed the teacher's religious objections.

Support infrastructure includes a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) offering helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland, which advises on legal sex and name changes, on the armed forces and on asylum.
tangentialFactors:
Blood donation rules moved on 1 November 2023 to a four-month deferral after the last new sexual contact for gay men, down from the one-year deferral applied since 2017.

UNHCR Switzerland records that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and that same-sex couples have been able to marry since 1 July 2022; this is relevant to protection claims, alongside the asylum advice offered by Transgender Network Switzerland.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map country page reports an overall index score and per-category compliance ratings for Switzerland, assessed after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes. The specific score values are not carried in the available source inventory.

A 2026 assessment summarises the Swiss regime as running from marriage equality to gender recognition with gaps remaining; the gaps it names in the inventory concern conversion therapy and federal detention rules rather than marker change itself.
localsOnly:
Residents benefit from a workplace duty that is already concretised: Art. 328ff. of the Code of Obligations obliges employers to protect personal dignity, and the Equality Act (GLG) applies it to trans employees, who may use a preferred name and gender on the job without updating official documents.

Detention placement is a cantonal matter, so conditions differ by canton. Basel-Stadt's JVG of 13 November 2019 is the explicit case where gender identity was written into a detention statute; the separation rules there permit deviation by the prison directorate in consultation with the referring authority.

Conversion therapy is banned only in some cantons: Neuchâtel since 2023, Valais and Vaud since 2024. The federal ban passed by the National Council on 12 December 2022 has not been enacted.

Residents in difficulty can reach a national helpline operating since November 2016, Dialogai for helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland for questions on legal sex and name change, on the armed forces and on asylum.

For families with trans minors, the age threshold for guardian consent to a marker change is the unsettled point between the two chambers of the Federal Assembly, so parents and guardians should confirm the current wording before applying.
